lexemes.note: Written attached to the next word. With the article it fuses: בְּ + הַבַּיִת → בַּבַּיִת (the ה falls away and its vowel moves to the ב: בַּ / בָּ / בֶּ). Its own vowel also changes: בִּ before a shva (בִּשְׂדֵה), בַּ before a hataf patah (בַּחֲנוּת).

profile.feeling: Where something is: in the house, at school, at work.

senses.def: at (a place: at school, at work, at the bank)
with, by means of (a tool): בְּעֵט “with a pen”
at (a time of day): בְּשָׁעָה חָמֵשׁ “at five o’clock”
in (a month, a season, a year; a part of the day): בְּמַאי, בַּקַּיִץ, בַּבֹּקֶר

examples.tr: The train leaves at five o’clock.
In January there is snow on Mount Hermon.

synonyms.nuance: “inside, within” — stresses that something is really inside: בְּתוֹךְ הָאָרוֹן

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *bV- “with, in, at, among”, possibly from Proto-Afroasiatic *bǔ “place” (Wiktionary). Arabic بِ (bi-) is the same prefix.

funFacts: Greek σε covers “in, at, to” at once — בְּ covers “in” and “at” (and “to” is לְ).
Arabic keeps the article after the same prefix (بِالْبَيْتِ bi-l-bayti); Hebrew swallows it (בַּבַּיִת).
English needs three words for time — at five, on Monday, in May; Hebrew uses בְּ for all three (German um, am, im).
pitfalls: With the article it fuses: בַּבַּיִת “in the house”, never *בְּהַבַּיִת.
Its vowel changes: בִּ before a shva (בִּשְׂדֵה תְּעוּפָה), בַּ before a hataf patah (בַּחֲנוּת).
It covers both “in” and “at”: בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר is “in the school” and “at school”.
Months take בְּ without the article (בְּמַאי), seasons and parts of the day with it (בַּקַּיִץ, בַּבֹּקֶר).
subtleties: Unvowelled בבית is both בְּבַיִת “in a house” and בַּבַּיִת “in the house, at home” — only the vowel shows the article.
A tool takes בְּ, not עִם: כּוֹתֵב בְּעֵט “writes with a pen”.

lexemes.note: At someone’s place: אֵצֶל סָבְתָא “at Grandma’s”, אֵצֶל הָרוֹפֵא “at the doctor’s”. With pronouns: אֶצְלִי, אֶצְלְךָ, אֶצְלָהּ …

profile.feeling: At Grandma’s, at the doctor’s, at a friend’s — the “at” of people (German bei, French chez).

senses.def: at (the home or office of a person): at someone’s
with, in the possession of (הַמַּפְתֵּחַ אֵצֶל אִמָּא “Mum has the key”)

synonyms.nuance: “in the house of …” — only for a home: בְּבֵית סָבְתָא

etymology.text: Biblical Hebrew, where it meant “beside, next to” (a meaning Wiktionary still lists); Wiktionary gives no etymology.

funFacts: German bei is the closest: bei Oma = אֵצֶל סָבְתָא, beim Arzt = אֵצֶל הָרוֹפֵא; French chez does the same job.
pitfalls: Only for people (and their homes or offices): “at school” is בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר, not *אֵצֶל בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר.
With pronouns the vowels change: אֶצְלִי, אֶצְלְךָ, אֶצְלֵךְ, אֶצְלוֹ, אֶצְלָהּ (Wiktionary).
subtleties: אֶצְלִי also means “in my case, with me”: אֶצְלִי זֶה אַחֶרֶת “with me it’s different”.

lexemes.role: “to, towards” — formal and written, mostly towards a person or a thing (אֶל הַחַלּוֹן “to the window”). The everyday “to” is the prefix לְ (known from יֵשׁ לִי): לַבַּיִת, לְאִמָּא.

profile.feeling: The “to” of letters, the Bible and careful speech.

senses.def: to, towards (a person or a thing)

synonyms.nuance: the everyday “to”, a prefix: לַבַּיִת, לְאִמָּא

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʾila “towards, nigh”, cognate with Akkadian ana and Arabic إِلَى (ʔilā) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic إِلَى (ʔilā) “to” is the same word.
pitfalls: In everyday speech use לְ: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לַבַּיִת, not אֶל הַבַּיִת.
With pronouns: אֵלַי “to me”, אֵלֶיךָ, אֵלָיו (Wiktionary).
subtleties: Unvowelled אל is also אַל “don’t!” and אֵל “god”.

lexemes.note: Written attached to the next word; the נ of the old form מִן doubles the next letter (מִתֵּל אָבִיב), and before a guttural, ר or the article it is מֵ (מֵחֵיפָה, מֵהַבַּיִת). The article does not fuse: מֵהַבַּיִת. The full word מִן stands before the article in careful style (מִן הַבַּיִת). In comparisons it is “than”: גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מֵהַדִּירָה (lesson 17).

profile.feeling: Where people and things come from.

senses.def: than (in comparisons): גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִ… “bigger than …”; before a clause or a phrase מֵאֲשֶׁר
of, out of (some of a group)
from, since (a point in time): מֵהַבֹּקֶר “since the morning”, מִשְּׁמוֹנֶה “from eight”

examples.tr: He has been here since Sunday.
I am at work from eight to five.
Jerusalem is bigger than Tel Aviv.

synonyms.nuance: “from (a person)” in formal letters: מִכְתָּב מֵאֵת הַמְּנַהֵל
“since” — only for time, also alone (“since then”): מֵאָז יָנוּאָר

etymology.text: From מִן (min), by assimilation of the n to the following consonant (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic مِنْ (min) “from”.

funFacts: Arabic مِنْ (min) is the same word — and Arabic keeps the n: مِنَ الْبَيْتِ.
In comparisons it means “than”: גָּדוֹל מִ… “bigger than …” (lesson 17) — like Arabic أَكْبَر مِنْ.
Greek από and Arabic مِنْ do the same double job: “from” and “than” (μεγαλύτερος από, أَكْبَرُ مِنْ).
pitfalls: The נ of מִן doubles the next letter: מִתֵּל אָבִיב (dagesh). Before ע, ח, א, ר and before the article it is מֵ: מֵחֵיפָה, מֵהַבַּיִת.
With the article it does not fuse: מֵהַבַּיִת (the ה stays) — unlike בַּבַּיִת and לַבַּיִת.
subtleties: The full word מִן is used before the article in careful style: מִן הַבַּיִת. Everyday speech says מֵהַבַּיִת.

As “than”, מִ takes endings with pronouns (מִמֶּנִּי “than me”, מִמְּךָ, מִמֶּנּוּ, מִמֶּנָּה, מֵהֶם), and before a clause, an adverb or a phrase with a preposition the full word מֵאֲשֶׁר is used: יוֹתֵר טוֹב מֵאֲשֶׁר בַּבַּיִת “better than at home”.

profile.feeling: Together: coffee with milk, dinner with friends.

senses.def: with (having): חֶדֶר עִם חַלּוֹן “a room with a window”

examples.tr: She is at the supermarket with her mother.
a room with a big window

synonyms.nuance: “together with” — emphatic or formal

etymology.text: Cognate with Ugaritic ʿm and, by metathesis, with Arabic مَعَ (maʕa) and Ugaritic mʿ (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The name עִמָּנוּאֵל (Immanuel) means “God is with us”: עִמָּנוּ + אֵל.
Arabic مَعَ (maʕa) has the same consonants in the other order (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: With a pronoun it takes another stem: אִתִּי, אִתְּךָ, אִתָּךְ (written איתי, איתך …); עִמִּי is literary.
A tool takes בְּ, not עִם: כּוֹתֵב בְּעֵט “writes with a pen”.
subtleties: Unvowelled עם is also עַם “a people, a nation” (עַם יִשְׂרָאֵל).

profile.feeling: Coffee without sugar, a day without work.

phrases.meaning: said after good news so that it lasts — like “touch wood”

synonyms.nuance: “without” in writing and on signs: לְלֹא תַּשְׁלוּם “free of charge”
“without” (literary), mostly with a pronoun: בִּלְעָדַיִךְ “without you (f.)”

etymology.text: Biblical Hebrew; Wiktionary gives no etymology.

funFacts: Yiddish speakers say keyn ayin hore for the same wish as בְּלִי עַיִן הָרָע.
pitfalls: It is one word, not בְּ + לִי “in me”.
No fusion with the article: בְּלִי הַתִּיק “without the bag”.
subtleties: בְּלִי + infinitive is “without doing”: בְּלִי לֶאֱכֹל “without eating”.

profile.feeling: A present for Mum, soup for the children.

examples.tr: Mum is cooking soup for the children.
I (m.) work in order to live.

synonyms.nuance: “for” in formal and written style
the short prefix “for, to”: זֶה לְךָ “this is for you”

etymology.text: From בְּ “in” + שְׁבִיל “path, trail (of)”: literally “in the trail of” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: שְׁבִיל is a path: “for you” is literally “in your path”.
pitfalls: Not “for” of time: “for two hours” is just שְׁעָתַיִם or בְּמֶשֶׁךְ שְׁעָתַיִם.
With pronouns: בִּשְׁבִילִי, בִּשְׁבִילְךָ, בִּשְׁבִילָהּ … (Wiktionary).
subtleties: בִּשְׁבִיל לְ… “in order to” is everyday speech; formal style says כְּדֵי לְ…

lexemes.note: “about” (a topic, lesson 11) and “on” (on top of, lesson 12) — one word. With pronouns: עָלַי, עָלֶיךָ, עָלָיו …

profile.feeling: A book about Jerusalem; the cup on the table.

examples.tr: This is a book about Jerusalem.
The book is on the table.
The glass is on the shelf.

synonyms.nuance: “about, concerning” — formal
“on top of” — formal

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʕalay- (Wiktionary); cognate with Arabic عَلَى (ʕalā) “on”.

funFacts: Arabic عَلَى (ʕalā) is the same word: عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ “on the table”.
German über does both jobs too: ein Buch über Jerusalem, das Bild über dem Sofa.
pitfalls: With pronouns it adds י: עָלַי “on me”, עָלֶיךָ, עָלָיו (Wiktionary).
It is a separate word: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן (no fusion with the article).
subtleties: עַל + a pronoun can mean “it is up to you, you must” (formal): עָלֶיךָ לְהַחְלִיט “you must decide”.

profile.feeling: School bags, the bell, the break in the yard.

examples.tr: The school is close to the house.

synonyms.nuance: a high school — short for בֵּית סֵפֶר תִּיכוֹן

etymology.text: From בַּיִת “house” + סֵפֶר “book” (Wiktionary); compare Akkadian bīt ṭuppim “house of the tablet”.

funFacts: Literally “house of book” — and Akkadian said bīt ṭuppim, “house of the tablet” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר “the school”; “at school” = בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר.
The plural changes the first word: בָּתֵּי סֵפֶר.
subtleties: A university is not a בֵּית סֵפֶר: it is an אוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הָאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה → (בַּ / לַ)אוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.

profile.feeling: Lecture halls, campus lawns and exams in the summer.

examples.tr: The students are at the university.
She studies at the Hebrew University.
There are two universities in the city.

synonyms.nuance: a college — usually smaller, teaching first degrees

etymology.text: An internationalism, borrowed from Western European languages; ultimately from Latin universitas (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem opened in 1925; Albert Einstein was one of its founders and left it his archive.
pitfalls: The plural keeps the א: אוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָאוֹת.
With the article: הָאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה; “at the university” = בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.
subtleties: Israelis study “in” the university: לוֹמְדִים בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הָעֲבוֹדָה → (בַּ / לַ)עֲבוֹדָה; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָעֲבוֹדָה.

profile.feeling: Work — the place you go to every morning, and the job itself.

examples.tr: I am at work until five.

phrases.meaning: idolatry; (humorously) a blind cult of something

synonyms.nuance: a position, a post — a job seen as a position
work, craft, a task (also the work forbidden on Shabbat)

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic عِبَادَة (ʕibāda) “worship” (Wiktionary); from the root ע־ב־ד “to work; to serve”.

funFacts: Arabic عِبَادَة means “worship” — the old sense of עֲבוֹדָה, the service in the Temple.
The Israeli Labor Party is called הָעֲבוֹדָה, “the Work” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: “At work” takes the article: בָּעֲבוֹדָה (literally “in the work”).
Before another noun it becomes עֲבוֹדַת: עֲבוֹדַת בַּיִת “homework”.
subtleties: The root ע־ב־ד also gives עֶבֶד “slave” and עוֹבֵד “employee”: work and service were one idea.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַמִּשְׂרָד → (בַּ / לַ)מִּשְׂרָד; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַמִּשְׂרָד.

profile.feeling: Desks, computers, meetings — and the ministries of the government.

examples.tr: She works in a government office.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; a study or work room at home is a חֲדַר עֲבוֹדָה.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it has the noun pattern מִקְטָל (Wiktionary) of many places, like מִטְבָּח “kitchen”.

funFacts: The Prime Minister’s Office is מִשְׂרַד רֹאשׁ הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה.
pitfalls: Before another noun the vowel shortens: מִשְׂרַד הַחוּץ.
The ש is a שׂ (s): mis-RAD.
subtleties: A ministry is also a מִשְׂרָד: מִשְׂרַד הַבְּרִיאוּת “the Ministry of Health”.

profile.feeling: Shop windows in the high street; the corner shop.

synonyms.nuance: a small grocery shop round the corner
a shopping mall — many shops under one roof

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic חָנוּתָא (ḥānūṯā) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic حَانُوت (ḥānūt) “shop” comes from the same Aramaic word.
pitfalls: Feminine, although it does not end in ־ָה: חֲנוּת קְטַנָּה.
Plural חֲנֻיּוֹת (written חנויות).
subtleties: “In a shop” and “in the shop” are both written בַּחֲנוּת: בְּ before a hataf patah becomes בַּ anyway.

profile.feeling: Trolleys, queues at the till before Shabbat.

examples.tr: I (m.) buy bread at the supermarket.
The supermarket is closed on Shabbat.

synonyms.nuance: the full word — on signs and in writing; its plural is סוּפֶּרְמַרְקֶטִים
a small corner grocery

etymology.text: From English super (Wiktionary), short for “supermarket”.

funFacts: German Supermarkt, Greek σουπερμάρκετ, Russian супермаркет — Israelis simply cut the internationalism to סוּפֶּר.
pitfalls: Unvowelled סופר is also סוֹפֵר “writer” and “counting”.
Everyday speech uses no plural of סוּפֶּר; for several, say סוּפֶּרְמַרְקֶטִים.
subtleties: As slang סוּפֶּר also means “super, very”: סוּפֶּר טָעִים “super tasty” (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Shouting sellers, piles of fruit, spices and noise.

examples.tr: We buy fruit at the market.

synonyms.nuance: a fair — a market held now and then

etymology.text: Probably from Akkadian sūqum “street”; compare Arabic سُوق (sūq) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic سُوق — the souk — is the same word.
pitfalls: Plural שְׁוָקִים (written שווקים).
Unvowelled שוק is also שׁוֹק “shin” and “shock”.
subtleties: In the Bible it is a street: בַּשְּׁוָקִים וּבָרְחֹבוֹת “in the streets and the squares” (Song of Songs 3:2).

profile.feeling: Eating out with friends — hummus places, grills, fish by the sea.

examples.tr: We are eating at the restaurant.

synonyms.nuance: an eating house, a simple diner

etymology.text: Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda from the root ס־ע־ד and the pattern מִקְטָלָה (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, the reviver of spoken Hebrew, coined the word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Before another noun it becomes מִסְעֶדֶת (Wiktionary): מִסְעֶדֶת דָּגִים.
“At the restaurant” = בַּמִּסְעָדָה (the מ doubles).
subtleties: The root ס־ע־ד means “to dine; to support”: סְעוּדָה is a festive meal.

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary writes the compound with a maqaf (בָּתֵּי־קָפֶה); the course writes the two words with a space, like its other compound nouns (בֵּית סֵפֶר, בֵּית חוֹלִים).

profile.feeling: Tel Aviv’s café life: a cappuccino on the pavement.

examples.text: יֵשׁ הַרְבֵּה בָּתֵּי קָפֶה בְּתֵל אָבִיב.
examples.tr: There are many cafés in Tel Aviv.

synonyms.nuance: in speech often just קָפֶה: נִפָּגֵשׁ בַּקָּפֶה “let’s meet at the café”

etymology.text: From בֵּית “house of” + קָפֶה “coffee”: literally “house of coffee” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German Kaffeehaus and Turkish kahvehane are built the same way: “coffee house”.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: בֵּית הַקָּפֶה; plural בָּתֵּי קָפֶה.
subtleties: Wiktionary writes it with a hyphen (maqaf): בֵּית־קָפֶה; with a space it is the same word.

profile.feeling: White corridors, doctors and worried visitors.

examples.tr: There is a hospital in the city.

collocations.tr: to be in hospital (“to lie in hospital”)

synonyms.nuance: a medical centre — the official name of many big hospitals

etymology.text: From בֵּית “house” + חוֹלִים “sick people, patients” (Wiktionary); it was common enough by 1778 to enter an Italian edition of Calepinus’s dictionary. Compare German Krankenhaus.

funFacts: German Krankenhaus is built the same way: “house of the sick” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The second word is a plural (“the sick”), and the article goes on it: בֵּית הַחוֹלִים.
Plural: בָּתֵּי חוֹלִים.
subtleties: Without the article, בְּבֵית חוֹלִים is “in hospital” (as a patient).

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary writes the compound with a maqaf (בָּתֵּי־מִרְקַחַת); the course writes the two words with a space, like its other compound nouns.

profile.feeling: Prescriptions, plasters and the on-duty pharmacy at night.

examples.tr: The pharmacy is open until ten.
There is a pharmacy next to the house.
The pharmacy is closed at night.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; the pharmacist is a רוֹקֵחַ (f. רוֹקַחַת).

etymology.text: From בֵּית “house of” + מִרְקַחַת (Wiktionary), the Biblical word for a mixed, perfumed ointment (Exodus 30:25).

funFacts: The Biblical perfumer who mixed the מִרְקַחַת was a רֹקֵחַ (Exodus 30:25) — the pharmacist is still called רוֹקֵחַ.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: בֵּית הַמִּרְקַחַת.
subtleties: מִרְקַחַת alone today means “jam”: מִרְקַחַת תּוּתִים “strawberry jam”.

profile.feeling: Accounts, cash machines, queues on Sunday morning.

examples.tr: There is a bank in the square.

etymology.text: Ultimately from Old Italian banca “counter, money-changer’s bench”, from Lombardic bank “bench”, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek τράπεζα (“table”) and Italian banca (“bench”) both name the money-changer’s table.
pitfalls: Only the money bank: a river bank is גָּדָה, a bench סַפְסָל.
“At the bank” = בַּבַּנְק.
subtleties: In Israel banks are open on Sunday — the first working day of the week.

profile.feeling: Parcels, stamps and a numbered queue ticket.

examples.tr: She is at the post office.

synonyms.nuance: the post-office branch — more precise than the bare הַדֹּאַר

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology for דֹּאַר “post”. The postman is a דַּוָּר and a stamp a בּוּל.

funFacts: E-mail is דֹּאַר אֶלֶקְטְרוֹנִי, shortened to דוא״ל.
pitfalls: The א is silent and the patah is said: DO-ar.
No plural in use for the post office; several are סְנִיפֵי דֹּאַר.
subtleties: One word for the service, the building and the letters: לָלֶכֶת לַדֹּאַר “to go to the post office”.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַתַּחֲנָה → (בַּ / לַ)תַּחֲנָה; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַתַּחֲנָה.

profile.feeling: Waiting for the bus at the stop; the busy central station.

examples.tr: There is a stop next to the house.
This is an important stage in life.

etymology.text: Revived from a reading of the Biblical hapax תַּחֲנֹתִי (2 Kings 6:8) as “camping place, stopping place”, from the root ח־נ־ה (compare חָנָה “to camp; to park”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The word was revived from a single Biblical verse (Wiktionary); a rival coinage, תַּחֲנוּת, did not catch on.
pitfalls: One word for a big station and a small stop.
Before another noun it becomes תַּחֲנַת: תַּחֲנַת רַכֶּבֶת.
subtleties: The root ח־נ־ה also gives חֲנָיָה “parking” and מַחֲנֶה “camp”.

profile.feeling: Departures, security checks and long hugs at Arrivals.

examples.tr: The airport is far from here.
There are several airports in the country.

synonyms.nuance: “flight harbour” — the official term: נְמַל הַתְּעוּפָה בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן
the abbreviation of נְמַל הַתְּעוּפָה בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן, Israel’s main airport

etymology.text: Literally “flight field”: שְׂדֵה, the construct form of שָׂדֶה “field”, + תְּעוּפָה “flight” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German Flughafen is a “flight harbour”, like the official נְמַל תְּעוּפָה; English airfield is a “flight field”, like שְׂדֵה תְּעוּפָה.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: שְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה; “at the airport” = בִּשְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה (בְּ before a shva becomes בִּ).
subtleties: The ש of שָׂדֶה is a שׂ (s).

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הָרְחוֹב → (בַּ / לַ)רְחוֹב; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָרְחוֹב.

profile.feeling: Addresses, traffic and children playing in the street.

senses.def: an open square (in old towns, Biblical)

examples.tr: The children are in the street.
My house is on Herzl Street.

synonyms.nuance: an avenue, a boulevard (שְׂדֵרוֹת רוֹטְשִׁילְד)
an alley, a lane

etymology.text: From the root of רָחַב “to be wide”, since it stood out in a town by being open and wide; Modern Hebrew shifted the meaning to “street” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The town of Rehovot (רְחוֹבוֹת) takes its name from the “wide places” of Genesis 26:22.
pitfalls: With the article the ר takes a qamats: הָרְחוֹב; “in the street” = בָּרְחוֹב.
Addresses: בִּרְחוֹב יָפוֹ “on Jaffa Street”.
subtleties: In the Bible a רְחוֹב was an open square where markets and trials were held (Wiktionary).

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַכִּכָּר → (בַּ / לַ)כִּכָּר; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַכִּכָּר.

profile.feeling: Fountains, demonstrations, cafés — and roundabouts on every road.

senses.def: a loaf (כִּכַּר לֶחֶם); a talent (an old weight)

examples.tr: There are many people in the square.
The bank is in the square.

synonyms.nuance: an open plaza, a forecourt (רַחֲבַת הַכֹּתֶל)

etymology.text: Compare כִּרְכָּר and Aramaic כַּכַּר (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In the Bible כִּכָּר is also a “talent” of silver or gold, a weight of 30–60 kg (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Feminine: כִּכָּר גְּדוֹלָה.
Written כיכר in full spelling.
subtleties: When you drive, כִּכָּר is a roundabout.

profile.feeling: Lawns, picnics and bicycles on a Saturday.

examples.tr: The children are in the park.
There is a park next to the house.

synonyms.nuance: a public garden — the older Hebrew term
a small neighbourhood park or garden

etymology.text: Borrowed from English park (Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry for it).

funFacts: German Park, Greek πάρκο, Russian парк, Turkish park — the same word in every language you know.
pitfalls: The א only marks the a: PARK, one syllable.
Plural פַּארְקִים.
subtleties: A small park in the neighbourhood, with swings, is a גִּנָּה or גִּנַּת שַׁעֲשׁוּעִים.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הָעִיר → (בַּ / לַ)עִיר; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָעִיר.
override.N;PL;DEF: Before an unstressed עָ the article is הֶ: הֶעָרִים (so in the Bible, e.g. Numbers 35:13); Wiktionary’s generated table gives הָעָרִים.

profile.feeling: Busy streets, buses and lights — the city.

examples.tr: Our house is in the city.
There are many cities in the country.

synonyms.nuance: a big city, a metropolis
a small town; the shtetl

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic ʿr “city” and perhaps Sumerian iri, uru “city”; the plural comes from an old word עָר of the same meaning (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The plural עָרִים comes from a different, old word, עָר (Wiktionary) — as if English “town” had the plural “cities”.
pitfalls: Feminine without a feminine ending: עִיר גְּדוֹלָה.
Irregular plural עָרִים; with the article הֶעָרִים.
subtleties: With the article: הָעִיר; “in the city” = בָּעִיר.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַכְּפָר → (בַּ / לַ)כְּפָר; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַכְּפָר.

profile.feeling: Quiet hills, orchards and a small grocery.

examples.tr: The village is small and pretty.
There are many villages in the Galilee.

synonyms.nuance: a farming village of family farms
a collective settlement

etymology.text: From Aramaic כַּפְרָא (kap̄rā) “village, open town”, from Akkadian kapru “farm, village”; compare Arabic كَفْر (kafr) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Capernaum is כְּפַר נַחוּם, “Nahum’s village”; Arabic place names with Kafr (كَفْر) use the same word.
pitfalls: After בְּ the כ loses its dot: בִּכְפָר (bichfar) “in a village”.
Before another noun: כְּפַר (כְּפַר סָבָא).
subtleties: Many place names begin with כְּפַר: כְּפַר סָבָא, כְּפַר תָּבוֹר.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הָאָרֶץ → (בַּ / לַ)אָרֶץ; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הָאָרֶץ.

profile.feeling: A land, a country — and, with the article, Israel itself.

examples.tr: The book fell to the ground.

synonyms.nuance: a state — a country as a political unit

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔarṣ́- (Wiktionary); cognate with Arabic أَرْض (ʔarḍ) “earth, land”.

funFacts: Abroad is חוּ״ל = חוּץ לָאָרֶץ, “outside the Land”.
Arabic أَرْض (ʔarḍ) is the same word.
הָאָרֶץ (“the Land”) is the name of one of Israel’s oldest daily newspapers.
pitfalls: Feminine: אֶרֶץ יָפָה.
With the article the vowels change: הָאָרֶץ (ha-A-rets); “in the Land” = בָּאָרֶץ.
subtleties: הָאָרֶץ alone usually means Israel: בָּאָרֶץ “in Israel”, חוּץ לָאָרֶץ “abroad”.

profile.feeling: Flags, borders, passports — the state.

examples.tr: California is a state in the United States.

synonyms.nuance: a land, a country (also: the earth); הָאָרֶץ is Israel

etymology.text: Likely borrowed from Aramaic מְדִינְתָּא (məḏīntā), from the root of דין “to judge” — the place where judgement is given; cognate with Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna) “city” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Medina in Arabia (الْمَدِينَة, “the city”) carries the same word (Wiktionary: cognate).
pitfalls: A false friend across the course: Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna) is a “city”, Hebrew מְדִינָה a “state”.
Before another noun it becomes מְדִינַת: מְדִינַת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
subtleties: מְדִינָה is the political state; אֶרֶץ is the land.
